concepts.title: A Torchlight: Source of the Idea

questions.q: What parts make a simple torch?
questions.a: Cells (battery), a bulb, a switch and connecting strips/wires in a case.

questions.q: Why does the torch light only when the switch is on?
questions.a: The switch completes the circuit so current can flow through the bulb.

questions.q: What happens if one cell is reversed in a torch?
questions.a: The cells may cancel and the bulb glows dimly or not at all.

questions.q: What does a simple electric circuit need to light a bulb?
questions.a: A source (cell), wires, and a bulb joined in an unbroken loop - a closed circuit.

questions.q: What is the path of current in a circuit?
questions.a: From the positive terminal of the cell through wires and bulb back to the negative terminal.

questions.q: Why must the two terminals of a cell never be joined by a bare wire alone?
questions.a: That shorts the cell - huge current drains it fast and can cause burns.

questions.q: Why do we use symbols in circuit diagrams?
questions.a: Standard symbols are quick to draw and understood by everyone, everywhere.

questions.q: Draw (describe) the symbol of a bulb and a switch.
questions.a: Bulb: a circle with a cross inside; switch: a gap in the line with a small lever.

questions.q: What does a dotted or open switch line show in a diagram?
questions.a: An open switch - the circuit is broken and no current flows.

questions.q: What are conductors and insulators? Give examples.
questions.a: Conductors let current pass (metals, graphite); insulators block it (plastic, rubber, wood).

questions.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic?
questions.a: Plastic is an insulator - it stops shocks and keeps current inside the wire.

questions.q: How does a switch use conductors and insulators?
questions.a: Its inner metal parts conduct when closed; the outer body insulates the hand.
